\section{Kings: The Tr\'ebuchet and When It Is Exact}\label{sec:kings}

So far a player with no pawn move simply lost. In chess that player would move the king instead, or, with no
king move either, be stalemated, which is a draw. The tr\'ebuchet of Section~\ref{sec:rules} removes
stalemate: a side with no pawn move must move a king, and loses. We now ask when this gives the true chess
result. Our king-and-pawn solver plays real chess, with en passant, stalemate and any of the four
promotions, but no fifty-move rule; an independent reference solver, written from the rules alone, agrees with
it on all $1{,}418{,}480$ positions of its test runs \lab{C2}. This validates the solver; its results below are
\lab{C1} unless a second program or the Lichess tablebase~\cite{LichessTB} confirms them.

\subsection{Two Tr\'ebuchets}

In Fig.~\ref{fig:trebuchet_2025} only the kings can move. White to move must give up a4, since the only square
next to a4 that the king on h5 can move to, h4, is attacked by the a5 pawn across the seam; black to move loses
a5 in the same way. Whoever moves first loses a pawn and then the game, so this is a zero game, and with the
kings played out a real mutual zugzwang that exists only because of the seam \lab{C2}.

Fig.~\ref{fig:trebuchet} shows the same idea on files f to h of the ordinary board; the Lichess tablebase
confirms that it is a mutual zugzwang \lab{C2}. We call this group T and place it beside every ordinary-board
pawn position in this paper.

\subsection{When Is the Frozen Tr\'ebuchet Exact?}\label{sec:kings-valid}

A \emph{king group} $Z$ is the two kings and some pawns on a block of files whose neighboring files, the
\emph{buffer}, hold no pawns; a \emph{decisive event} is a move that creates a passed pawn, or a move in $Z$.

\begin{theorem}[Validity of the convention; \lab{AI}]\label{thm:validity}
Let a position consist of pawn components and a king group $Z$ with its buffer, and suppose that before the
first decisive event:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(V1)] the legal chess moves are exactly the moves of the model, nobody is in check, and the side to move
  has a legal move;
\item[(V2)] the side that gets a passed pawn wins;
\item[(V3)] every move in $Z$ is decisively punished.
\end{enumerate}
Then the chess result, with either side to move, is the normal-play outcome of the components, without draws.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By (V3) the model is the normal-play sum of the components, without draws; its winner never moves in $Z$, and by
(V1) the loser has only model moves, so play ends at a decisive event that wins the chess game for the winner by
(V2) and (V3). The full proof is in the repository.
\end{proof}

\begin{conjecture}[\lab{Conj}]\label{conj:v4}
If also (V4) the pawn part is hereditarily sum-safe (Definition~\ref{def:hss}) and $\BIG$ exceeds every tempo
count, the chess result in Theorem~\ref{thm:validity} is the outcome class of the $\pm\BIG$ value of the
components.
\end{conjecture}

A proof, repaired after review and building on Theorem~\ref{thm:hss}, is in the repository; it has been
checked only by AI models, so we state the result as a conjecture. Each condition can fail: a king walks over to the pawns (V1),
a passed pawn does not win its race (V2), white's king moves in Fig.~\ref{fig:kinggroup72} go unpunished (V3),
and a $+\BIG$ cancels a $-\BIG$ (V4; Section~\ref{sec:sums-hss}).

A local test for (V3) is the \emph{certificate of horizon $h$}: with all other pawns removed, the punisher
promotes within $h$ moves of its reply even if the defender may pass at any time, the defender cannot promote
anywhere within $h$ moves (the \emph{counter-promotion condition}), and the defender is never stalemated.

\begin{conjecture}[\lab{Conj}]\label{conj:cert}
A certificate of horizon $h$ implies (V3).
\end{conjecture}

Our proof of this has a gap.

\begin{proposition}[\lab{AI}]\label{prop:horizon1}
On boards with at least six ranks, for $h=1$, the counter-promotion condition holds in every context without a
passed pawn.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A pawn that can promote in one move stands on the rank before its last. With six or more ranks it got there by a
single step or a capture, so it cannot be taken en passant, and no enemy pawn can stand ahead of it: it is
already passed.
\end{proof}

\begin{conjecture}[\lab{Conj}]\label{conj:horizon2}
For every king group whose punishment needs $h\ge2$ moves, some context without a passed pawn leaves a move in
the group unpunished.
\end{conjecture}

Real tr\'ebuchets need $h\approx5$--$7$, so we trust their zero only beside slow or locked components.

\subsection{Spare King Moves Are Loopy}

A king that can step back and forth without loss gives its side unlimited waiting moves, a loopy
game~\cite{WinningWays,Siegel2013}: $\textsf{on}=\game{\textsf{on}}{}$ if only white can wait,
$\textsf{off}=-\textsf{on}$ if only black can, and $\textsf{dud}$ if both can. Since $\textsf{on}$ exceeds every number, $\BIG$ included, the $\pm\BIG$ convention fails there, and a
decisive event must instead end the game.

\begin{theorem}[Outcomes with spare moves; \lab{AI}]\label{thm:loopy}
Let every decisive event end the game. If only white can wait, black wins exactly when it can force a decisive
event in its favor against a white who may pass at any time; otherwise white wins. If both can wait, either side
wins exactly when it can do so against a passing opponent; otherwise the game is drawn.
\end{theorem}

Beside a spare king move, then, component values matter only through their forcing threats.

\subsection{How Often Does the Convention Fail?}\label{sec:kings-sweep}

We solved, with the kings played out, every component with at most two pawns a side beside a
tr\'ebuchet on boards with six ranks: on one file of the six-file cylinder and of the five-file ordinary board,
and on files d and e of the seven-file cylinder (queen promotions only, at most two; on the six-file cylinder
the all-promotion results agree in $42$ of $42$ cases). Of these, $500$ start without a race and have a
determined result. Under the textbook test, $159$ of the $500$ get the wrong outcome \lab{C1}: $107$ through
the kings alone, $18$ through en passant and $34$ because a passed pawn does not win its race. $143$ of the
$159$ are on the seven-file cylinder. The e.p.-aware test repairs the convention in the $18$ e.p.\ failures,
but in $13$ of them the free kings change the result again, so the count there falls only from $143$ to
$138$. On the ordinary $8\times8$ board we checked $94$ positions beside a tr\'ebuchet against the
tablebase. The convention says every one of their $449$ king moves loses, yet $41$ of them draw and $7$ win
\lab{C1}.
